what: Apply the allmänfarlig and samhällsfarlig provisions of smittskyddslagen to covid-19, by regulation
why: Förordning 2020:20, decided 1 February 2020 under chapter 2 section 9 of smittskyddslagen (2004:168) and in force from 2 February. Classification unlocks mandatory reporting, contact tracing and powers over infected individuals. The permanent listing in the Act's appendices followed later, from 1 July 2020. This is the enabling step everything else rests on, and it was taken five weeks before the first restriction.
source: Regeringen klassar coronavirus som samhällsfarlig sjukdom (Krisinformation.se)

what: The government had no legal mandate for a general lockdown
why: Chapter 2 of the Instrument of Government protects freedom of movement, and neither existing legislation nor emergency-powers doctrine gave the government authority for a nationwide lockdown in peacetime. Much of what looks like a chosen strategy was, at least in part, the only lawful option available at the time.
source: Sweden's constitution decides its exceptional Covid-19 policy (CEPR)

what: Ban public gatherings of more than 500 people
why: First binding national restriction. Chosen as a proportionate limit on mass events while leaving daily life, workplaces and schools untouched. References SE-2020-02-01-001.
source: COVID-19 pandemic in Sweden

what: WHO characterises covid-19 as a pandemic
why: The international backdrop against which every national choice below was made, and the same day Sweden banned gatherings over 500.
source: COVID-19 pandemic in Sweden

what: Govern the pandemic through non-binding recommendations rather than legal mandates
why: Sweden leaned on allmänna råd and personal responsibility, on the reasoning that measures people accept voluntarily can be sustained for the long haul, and that trust in institutions makes advice work without coercion. This is the choice everything else in 2020 follows from, and it is inseparable from the legal constraint the government was operating under. References SE-2020-03-01-901, SE-2020-03-11-001, SE-2020-02-01-001.
source: Sweden: Non-binding Rules against the Pandemic (European Journal of Risk Regulation)

what: Move upper secondary schools and universities to distance learning
why: Older students can study remotely without requiring a parent to leave work. The measure reduces contacts without the knock-on effects of closing schools for younger children. References SE-2020-03-11-001.
source: The first eight months of Sweden's COVID-19 strategy (Ludvigsson, Acta Paediatrica 2020)

what: Keep schools open for children up to age 16, and keep kindergartens open, for the whole pandemic
why: Closing schools was judged to carry large costs for children's welfare and learning, and to remove healthcare staff from work to provide childcare, while the evidence for children as major drivers of transmission was considered weak. This is the single most internationally conspicuous Swedish choice. References SE-2020-03-17-001.
source: The first eight months of Sweden's COVID-19 strategy (Ludvigsson, Acta Paediatrica 2020)

what: Lower the limit on public gatherings from 500 to 50
why: Tightening as case numbers climbed, while still stopping short of a general lockdown. References SE-2020-03-11-001.
source: COVID-19 pandemic in Sweden

what: Prohibit visits to residential care homes for older people
why: Elderly care residents were dying in large numbers. The ban was the most intrusive national measure taken in 2020, and it was aimed at the group the strategy was failing. References SE-2020-03-27-001, SE-2020-02-01-001.
source: Sweden: Legal Response to Covid-19 (Oxford Constitutional Law)

what: Publicly declare the strategy a failure and call on politicians to take over from the agency
why: Headline: 'Folkhälsomyndigheten har misslyckats. Nu måste politikerna gripa in.' The authors noted that between 7 and 9 April more people per million had died in Sweden than in Italy, and ten times more than in Finland, and wrote that agency officials had shown no talent for predicting or limiting the epidemic. References SE-2020-04-01-001, SE-2020-03-17-002.
source: Sweden: 22 Scientists Say Coronavirus Strategy Has Failed (Forbes)

what: Reject the criticism, disputing both the authors' standing and their use of the data
why: Tegnell said the authors were not leaders in their field and had cherrypicked the days with the highest death tolls. Commentators also disputed the figures. Tegnell responded publicly in the days immediately following publication; the exchange, not its precise hour, is what the record turns on. References SE-2020-04-14-001.
source: Critics of Sweden's lax pandemic policies face fierce backlash (Science)

what: Expand testing sharply and make it free for everyone with symptoms
why: Testing moved from prioritised groups only to large-scale national testing of anyone symptomatic. Sweden's testing was slow to scale, a consequence of responsibility being split between the state, 21 regions and the agency, which the research literature identifies as a structural cause rather than a single bad call. References SE-2020-03-16-001.
source: COVID-19 Testing in Sweden During 2020: Split Responsibilities and Multi-Level Challenges (Frontiers in Public Health)

what: Announce the lifting of the national care-home visiting ban, effective 1 October
why: Reversed on the grounds that isolation was itself harming residents. The most intrusive measure of 2020 was also the first undone. References SE-2020-04-01-001.
source: Sweden to lift ban on visits to elderly care homes (The Local)

what: Permit local visiting bans at care homes again
why: Seven weeks after the national ban ended, the power to close homes to visitors returned in local form as the second wave hit. A decision reversed, then partly re-reversed, inside two months. References SE-2020-09-15-001, SE-2020-11-24-001.
source: Sweden permits local bans on visiting elderly care homes (The Local)

what: Cut the limit on public gatherings to eight people
why: Announced 16 November, in force 24 November, initially for four weeks, as the second wave broke. Made under the Public Order Act, so this was binding law with fines or up to six months' imprisonment, not a recommendation. The sharpest reversal of the spring posture. References SE-2020-03-27-001, SE-2020-03-16-001.
source: Sweden bans public events of more than eight people (The Local)

what: First interim report: the strategy to protect the elderly has failed
why: SOU 2020:80, 'Äldreomsorgen under pandemin'. The commission found elderly care was unprepared and ill-equipped because of structural defects known before the outbreak, and held that the current and previous governments bear ultimate responsibility for them. References SE-2020-04-01-001.
source: Summary of SOU 2020:80 Elderly care during the pandemic (Government.se)

what: Begin vaccination, prioritising care-home residents and the staff around them
why: Supply was short, so the programme ran in three phases with residents of elderly homes and their carers first. The group the strategy had failed in the spring was placed at the front of the queue. References SE-2020-12-15-001.
source: Covid-19 vaccination begins on 27 December (Krisinformation.se)

what: Recommend face masks on public transport at rush hour, reversing a year of advice against them
why: In force 7 January 2021, for people born before 2004, on weekdays 07:00 to 09:00 and 16:00 to 18:00, and only where distance could not be kept. Medical CE-marked masks specified, cloth masks explicitly not recommended. Until this point Sweden had resisted masks outside healthcare, so this is the clearest documented reversal in the record. References SE-2020-11-24-001, SE-2020-03-16-001.
source: Masks in public transport from 7 January (Krisinformation.se)

what: Adopt a temporary covid-19 act granting broader powers to restrict
why: Passed in a special session and in force from 10 January 2021. It supplied the legal authority the government had lacked in 2020, alongside the Public Order Act and the Communicable Diseases Act. References SE-2020-03-01-901, SE-2020-11-24-001.
source: Sweden: New COVID-19 Act Enters into Force (Library of Congress)

what: Responsibility was split three ways, between the state, 21 self-governing regions and an independent agency
why: Swedish agencies operate at arm's length from ministers, and healthcare is run by the regions. Much of what outsiders read as a national strategy was the output of a system with no single decision-maker, which matters for any question about who was answerable. References SE-2020-03-01-901, SE-2020-06-04-001.
source: Evaluation of science advice during the COVID-19 pandemic in Sweden (Nature HSSC)

what: Second interim report: the response in early 2020 was insufficient and late
why: SOU 2021:89 'Sverige under pandemin', dated 18 October and delivered 29 October 2021. It found the handling characterised by lateness, with initial protective measures insufficient to stop or even significantly limit spread. References SE-2020-03-16-001, SE-2020-12-15-001.
source: SOU 2021:89 Sverige under pandemin, Volym 1 (Regeringen)

what: Announce that nearly all restrictions end on 9 February 2022
why: Andersson: 'The pandemic is not over, but is entering a completely new phase.' Reasoning given was high vaccination coverage, milder Omicron outcomes and falling intensive care admissions. Vaccine passes, the mask recommendation on transport and limits on gatherings all went at once. References SE-2020-12-27-001, SE-2021-01-08-001, SE-2020-12-30-001.
source: Sweden to lift nearly all Covid-19 restrictions next week (The Local)

what: Final report: the strategy was fundamentally correct, and the measures were too weak and too late
why: SOU 2022:10, 'Sverige under pandemin'. The commission held that relying on voluntary measures rather than lockdown was fundamentally correct, in part for preserving personal freedom, while criticising the failure to take more rigorous measures in February and March 2020. By publication 15,800 people had died, 1.5 per 1000 inhabitants. References SE-2020-03-17-002, SE-2020-04-14-001, SE-2020-03-01-901, SE-2020-12-15-001, SE-2020-12-30-001.
source: KEY POINTS: The final verdict on Sweden's Covid-19 response (The Local)

what: Excess mortality across 2020 and 2021 was +0.79%, lower than in many European countries, while spring 2020 death rates were high
why: The two facts sit together and are usually cited apart. Which one you lead with determines the story you tell, and that is exactly what the piece should make visible rather than resolve. References SE-2022-02-25-001.
source: How Sweden approached the COVID-19 pandemic (Ludvigsson, Acta Paediatrica 2023)

what: About 88 percent of Swedish covid deaths were among people aged 70 or over
why: Socialstyrelsen recorded 14,703 deaths with covid among people aged 70 or over between 1 March 2020 and 31 March 2022, against 1,928 under 70, so roughly 88 percent of deaths fell in the oldest group. The corrective matters as much as the figure: the share was above 80 percent in all four Nordic countries, so the concentration among the old was not distinctively Swedish. What the commission found distinctive was the state of elderly care itself. References SE-2020-12-15-001, SE-2022-02-25-001.
source: Statistics on COVID-19 (Socialstyrelsen)
